awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Metasurface Optical Waveguides for Compact and Scalable Optical Systems
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial impacts of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is in replacing conventional optical systems, like  lenses, mirrors, or their combinations, that need to be individually produced, assembled, aligned, and placed within a housing or enclosure.  Such optical systems are used in smart phones, consumer wearables devices, biometric identification, medical diagnostics, autonomous navigation, robotics, remote sensing, etc.  This project will develop novel optical devices that will overcome the limitations of traditional optical systems with respect to weight, size, scalability, and cost. The system will be composed of tiny features that interact with light on a sub-wavelength scale. Development of the novel optical devices will directly benefit U.S. consumers. The innovation is expected to transform a variety of optical and photonic systems into lighter, more affordable, and more compact solutions that can be produced in large volumes. 

This Small Business Innovative Research (SBIR) Phase I project develops innovative metasurface optical waveguiding devices (MOWGs) that control light on a subwavelength level and will provide significant practical benefits over a variety of conventional optical systems. Conventional optical systems contain assemblies of optical components, such as refractive lenses, mirrors, or their combinations, that need to be individually fabricated, assembled, aligned, and placed within a housing or enclosure. That results in relatively bulky and heavy optical assemblies that have limited potential for cost reduction and scalability. Metasurfaces represent a new class of optical surface that control optical fields on the sub-wavelength level. Novel metasurface topologies that can be applied to optical waveguides will be explored.  This SBIR Phase I project is intended to overcome the limitations of traditional optical systems with respect to weight, size, scalability, and cost by employing metasurface assemblies containing waveguiding structures.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report

Coherent Photonics completed an NSF SBIR Phase I project focused on assessing the feasibility of a new class of compact, low-size, weight, and power metasurface-enabled optical sensing systems. The project addressed key limitations of conventional optical sensing architectures, including excessive size and weight, limited scalability, and high manufacturing cost. The proposed approach uses engineered metasurface waveguides to couple, guide, and redirect light in a compact optical module that can potentially replace larger multi-element optical systems.

During the Phase I effort, Coherent Photonics developed system-level and component-level optical models of the metasurface waveguide-based sensing architecture. These models were used to evaluate how light from different incoming directions can be routed through a metasurface waveguide and directed toward selected pixels of a photosensitive array. The modeled architecture combines a metasurface waveguide, metalens, and sensor array to create a compact optical sensing module. Compared with a conventional multi-element optical sensing system, the proposed architecture is projected to provide substantial reductions in optical weight and high-volume manufacturing cost, enabled by wafer-level fabrication and monolithic integration.

A central technical outcome of the project was the design and optimization of the key metasurface waveguiding component. Coherent Photonics used rigorous electromagnetic simulation methods, including Finite Difference Time Domain and Rigorous Coupled Wave Analysis, together with advanced machine-learning-based optimization methods. This work produced free-form sub-wavelength metasurface topologies with improved simulated diffraction efficiency compared with conventional grating approaches. The optimized design achieved a simulated first-order diffraction efficiency of 97.3%. The optimized designs were translated into GDSII CAD layouts suitable for prototype fabrication.

The project also advanced the company’s design-for-manufacturing capability for metasurface optics. Tolerance analysis showed that high optical efficiency depends strongly on the shape and dimensional accuracy of individual nanoscale metasurface features. The Phase I work identified dimensional tolerance requirements on the order of approximately ±10 nanometers for near-nominal optical performance. This finding helped define the fabrication-control requirements needed for future development.

With NSF approval of a no-cost extension, Coherent Photonics expanded the Phase I scope by fabricating and experimentally characterizing metasurface waveguide feasibility prototypes, an activity originally planned for Phase II. The fabricated prototypes were tested in Coherent Photonics’ nano-photonics characterization laboratory. Testing confirmed optical coupling, guided-wave propagation, and out-coupling in the fabricated metasurface waveguide prototype. This result increased the technology maturity from Technology Readiness Level 2 to Technology Readiness Level 3.

The project also identified specific areas for future improvement, including predictive modeling of fabrication-induced topology changes, optical loss reduction, improved process control, surface-roughness reduction, and design-for-manufacturing optimization. Coherent Photonics began developing a data-driven workflow to compare fabricated nanoscale structures with nominal CAD layouts and use those data to improve future designs. This workflow is expected to support pre-corrected CAD layouts, optical proximity correction, and a metasurface-specific process design kit.

Beyond technical feasibility, the Phase I project strengthened the company’s commercialization foundation. Coherent Photonics completed NSF I-Corps customer discovery, conducted more than 100 customer interviews, entered discussions with prospective customers, and received several external endorsements. The Phase I work also contributed to the company’s intellectual-property portfolio through a patent application covering high-efficiency free-form sub-wavelength metasurface topologies.

Overall, the NSF SBIR Phase I project successfully demonstrated the feasibility of metasurface-enabled optical waveguiding sensors and established a clear path toward Phase II development. The work produced validated models, optimized metasurface designs, fabrication-ready layouts, prototype characterization data, and a defined roadmap for advancing toward an integrated sensing prototype. Future development will focus on improving fabricated-device efficiency, reducing optical losses, refining fabrication processes, integrating the waveguide with detector and optical subsystems, and validating a compact sensor prototype in a relevant environment.
